title: Kiddie Katch-A-Bus rolls again — new gears, handmade belt, glued rollers
description: This motorized Kiddie Katch-A-Bus had three separate faults. Cracked gears were replaced in its tiny gearbox, the perished rubber belt was remade by hand until the tension was right, and cracked rollers in the dock were glued so the release button works again.
itemDetails: Kiddie Katch-A-Bus is a motorized playset sold as "A Child Guidance Toy." The box says it was manufactured in Japan for Child Guidance Products, Inc. of the Bronx, New York, and it carries the Questor logo. Questor brought Child Guidance into its educational toy business around 1969, and a 1970s toy reference lists Kiddie Katch-A-Bus in 1970, so this set dates from about that time. The set has a yellow bus with a clear roof and a smiling face on the front, a blue oval track, two automatic bus stops, and eight peg-style passengers. It runs on one C battery. The bus drives around the track and stops at a dock. A lever then shifts the motor's power from the wheels to a belt inside the chassis, which moves the passengers through the bus. Pressing the button on the dock releases the bus to drive on to the next stop.
repairDetails: The bus did not work when it arrived, and the repair turned up three separate problems. The first was in the gearbox. Several gears had cracked, so the small motor could no longer drive the wheels. The whole gearbox came apart piece by piece, the damaged gears were replaced, and everything was lined up and reassembled. The bus then went on the track for a gearbox test before any work started on the belt. The second was the rubber belt that moves the passengers along the chassis. The original had perished, so a new one was made by hand, cut to length and joined into a loop. Too loose or too tight and it will not work, so it took multiple tries to get the tension right. Glue holds the final join. The third was the release button on the dock. The bus is meant to stop there while the passengers transfer, but the button could no longer send it off again. The rollers inside the dock had cracked. The dock was opened, the rollers came out, and the cracks were glued back together. With the dock and bus reassembled, the bus stops, the belt moves the passengers, and the button sends it on its way.

googleReview.quote:
I bought a vintage toy on ebay with huge nostalgia from my childhood. I paid a lot of money to get it sent from overseas with the promise that it was in working order. It wasn't. Hugely disappointed and feeling duped, I let it sit in my wardrobe for about a year. Then I found THE TOY DOCTOR. Grace said she'd give it a go. It took 6 months, but Grace took the toy apart, assessed what was needed, ordered specific replacement parts, and never once questioned my desire and wish to have this toy back to use and be as thrilled about as i was as a kid. Then mailed it back to me and charged such a minimal amount that I'm sure her hours of work were more for love than money.

She is an absolute genius and a magician.

I no longer feel foolish for purchasing the toy, as she fixed it and my grandkids and I will get many hours of joy from it in years to come. She saved my toy and gave me dignity and joy back.
